Ooh, I got some speculation on my article. Cool. However, that wasn't something I particularly wanted to happen with this article. So, I feel this would be a relevant time to share this for those that haven't caught on.

This is my much simpler explanation/headcanon as to what happened with this -EX. (SPOILERS)
A small exoplanet with alien life on it collided with a larger planet.

Totally not assuming you didn't already think this, by the way. As you said, your theory isn't your headcanon. Previous critters have had similar confusion on the intended plot of this scip though, so this is just in case more people were stumped on this than I thought. Headcanon whatever you wish though, of course.

Edit: As for the pixelated image, I see where you're coming from, but both images use the same 3D model and texture. The pixelation I applied just simplified the shape and coloring that way.

item.content:encoded:
I have a bit of a crazy theory.

But that's just a theory.
A GAME-- er, wait, no-- SCP theory.

The two images presented to us in the article are of very similar appearance, but they are, obviously, not the same. Analysis of the 'pupil' indicated that it was an impact with either a very large asteroid or some other exoplanet.

Yes, the 1999 photo is low quality with understandable reasoning for said quality. But, don't you think that we'd at least see a little bit of the oddly-shaped ring of sulfur being… well, oddly-shaped instead of perfectly circular as it is in the photo. Yes, the quality is bad due to the technology, but I don't think it would still be seen as a perfect circle.

Here's where the crazy bit comes in. The reason why that ring is perfectly circular in that photo is that it was perfectly circular. Even during its appearance as a human eyeball, it sustained alien life. But that alien life had a bit of an internal conflict, just as we have had on multiple occasions here on Earth.

War.

Weapons of mass destruction were used during this war, causing the previously-perfect ring to be spread out by the large wave caused by the explosion. That is why the odd, vaguely-shaped ring currently present on SCP-1094-EX is shaped as it is as compared to the first chronological photo in the article.

Yes, this is obviously a very flawed theory, as the counterargument as "how/why was it an eyeball to begin with?" I don't have an answer to that, unfortunately.

This isn't my headcanon for the object, but it's just a little something I thought of. I figured it would be pretty cool to share it with you guys.


Yeah, it's pretty far-fetched, but I think it's a possibility.

Word, I get that. But even if it was moving at half the speed of light the entire time it was traveling (which obviously doesn't account for the ramp up and down time it would take to get to that speed) you're still cutting it pretty close to 2999, which is the last date that makes sense there.

And honestly, even if it did get there in that amount of time, it would take another four hundred and some years for us to even get any information about it back, since you can't move a signal faster than the speed of light. You're now talking like, 1500 years of investment into this thing. It's hard to say if the Foundation would be around in another 300 years, let alone five times that.

Let me say again, I do really like this. It's a neat vibe and those images are pretty baller. But letting the reader make their own assumption, in this case, is not particularly helpful, because my assumption initially was that you botched the math, or forgot to remark that the probe was anomalous or using wormholes or something. If it's a wormhole thing that definitely changes the game here a bit, but again, I'd probably want to mention that were I you.

item.content:encoded:
I like this. One pretty major issue, though.

You indicate that SCP-1094-EX is at least 484LY from Earth, which tracks. You then indicate that the Foundation sent out a probe to check it out, which left in 20021. You then later indicate that the probe arrived on 12/10/2███, which I imagine is intended to give us the indication that a considerable amount of time had passed. This also tracks.

Except if the probe was moving, let's say, twice the speed of Voyager 1 (roughly 80,000mph), it would still take the probe 4,057,230 years to get there. That date is missing some blackboxes.

In other words, either the planet was a lot close than we anticipated (a lot closer, mind you), or the probe was moving anomalously fast, in which case you'd probably want to mention that.

Footnotes
1. I honestly don't care for future Foundation, but I'll give it a pass here
